neighbors.heading: every syllable in tune
neighbors.text: Today tiny marks told a reader how to chant the Torah. Hindu tradition guards the sound of the Vedas closely too. The Taittiriya Upanishad opens a lesson on how to say the holy words: the letters, the pitch accent, the length, the effort, the evenness, the joining of sounds. (paraphrase) Students learn the chant by ear, line by line, from a teacher.
neighbors.difference: The Torah's notes are written above and below the letters in printed Bibles, and the scroll stays bare. The Vedas were long carried by voice alone, teacher to student, and the sound itself is held sacred.
neighbors.shared: how you say the holy words is part of what they mean.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.2, the lesson on pronunciation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: recite it slowly
neighbors.text: Today tiny marks told a reader how to chant the Torah. Muslims recite the Qur'an aloud with the same care. The Qur'an itself asks for it: recite the Qur'an slowly, in measured, distinct tones. (paraphrase) The rules for reciting well are called tajwid: where to stretch a vowel, where to pause, where to stop.
neighbors.difference: The Torah's chant follows marks set over each word, learned in advance. Tajwid gives rules for sound and pausing, and a reciter may carry them on a melody of their own.
neighbors.shared: a holy book is meant to be heard, not only read.

items.lessonTitle: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)

neighbors.heading: others were tortured
neighbors.text: Today a mother watched her seven sons refuse to break the laws of their fathers, and she encouraged them. Christians remember faithful people like these in the Letter to the Hebrews. Its roll call of faith says: "others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection." Some readers hear this mother's sons in that line.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the brothers die holding to the Torah's commandments. Hebrews gathers such witnesses as people who trusted God's promise before Christ came, and some Christian Bibles include the Maccabees' story itself.
neighbors.shared: courage can pass from one heart to another in a single word.

neighbors.heading: a grandmother's courage
neighbors.text: Today a mother encouraged her sons to stay faithful, even to death. Sikhs remember a grandmother in a cold tower. Mata Gujri, mother of Guru Gobind Singh, was held at Sirhind with her two youngest grandsons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh. Sikhs tell that she urged them to stand firm. Offered their lives if they gave up their faith, the boys refused, and were killed.
neighbors.difference: The mother in Maccabees speaks of a Creator who will give her sons breath again. Sikhs remember the young Sahibzade as martyrs of the Guru's path, and gather at Fatehgarh Sahib, where they died, to honor them.
neighbors.shared: a child stands taller when someone they love says, stay true.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of Mata Gujri and the younger Sahibzade at Sirhind (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: altar and table
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis set the altar down in the kitchen: a table that feeds guests does the altar's work. Catholics join altar and table too. The Church teaches that the altar at Mass is both the altar of the sacrifice and the table of the Lord, where people gather to be fed. A psalm says it: "Thou hast prepared a table before me."
neighbors.difference: For the rabbis, the home table takes up the altar's work, through hospitality to guests and the hungry. For Catholics, the altar's table is the Eucharist itself, where they believe Christ gives himself as food.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal can be holy ground.
neighbors.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1383 (paraphrase) · Psalm 22:5 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 23:5 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: the gift of food
neighbors.text: Today the rabbis said a table becomes holy through who gets a seat. Buddhists hold the gift of food close to the heart of practice. In one teaching, the Buddha tells a laywoman that whoever gives food gives four things: long life, beauty, happiness and strength, and shares in those same four. (paraphrase) In some places, monks walk each morning with bowls, and households fill them.
neighbors.difference: The rabbis say a table that feeds the hungry atones, standing in for the altar. Buddhists call giving dana, generosity: a practice that loosens the grip of greed and plants good for the giver.
neighbors.shared: the measure of a meal is who gets to eat it.

neighbors.heading: the last words
neighbors.text: Today Rabbi Akiva died saying the Shema, the words he had said every morning and evening. Muslims hope for something like it: that their last words will be the words of oneness, la ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but God. The Prophet said that whoever's last words are these will enter Paradise. (paraphrase) Families gently say them at a deathbed.
neighbors.difference: Akiva died a martyr, keeping the command to love God with all his soul. The Muslim hope is for any death, peaceful or hard, and the words are the first half of the shahada, the witness of faith.
neighbors.shared: the words you say every day can carry you at the end.

neighbors.heading: practicing for the end
neighbors.text: Today Akiva found that a phrase he had studied all his life fit the hardest hour of it. Philosophers have spoken of a whole life as practice too. In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates spends his last day talking with friends, then drinks the poison calmly. He tells them that those who truly love wisdom spend their lives practicing for death. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Akiva's steadiness comes from love of the one God, said in the words of the Shema. Socrates' comes from philosophy: his trust that the soul and the search for truth outlast the body.
neighbors.shared: what you practice daily is what you'll have when it counts.

neighbors.heading: never in the trash
neighbors.text: Today a storeroom in Cairo kept every worn page with God's name on it, because holy words aren't thrown away. Sikhs care for a worn copy of the Guru Granth Sahib with the same reverence. A saroop too old to read from is never thrown out. It is carried with respect and cremated, the way a beloved person would be. Sikhs call this agan bhet, an offering to fire.
neighbors.difference: Jewish tradition stores worn holy books and in time buries them, like a person. Sikhs cremate them, as Sikhs cremate their dead. For Sikhs the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, so its care is care for the Guru.
neighbors.shared: words that carried something holy deserve a gentle goodbye.
neighbors.sources: the Sikh practice of agan bhet for worn saroops (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: given back to the river
neighbors.text: Today a storeroom in Cairo kept every worn page with God's name on it. Hindu homes have a custom like it. When a holy book falls apart, or an image of a god is cracked or worn, it isn't tossed in the trash. It is often given to flowing water, a river or the sea, with a prayer, or laid in clean earth.
neighbors.difference: In Cairo, keeping worn writings saved a community's memory, though no one planned it. The Hindu custom returns holy things to nature, so the river and the earth receive what was honored at home.
neighbors.shared: what was holy in your hands stays holy when you let it go.
neighbors.sources: Hindu custom of visarjan, immersing worn sacred images and books (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: places to see once
neighbors.text: Today Judah Halevi wrote that his heart was in the east, and then he packed. Buddhists know that pull toward a place. Near his death, the Buddha named four places a person of faith should see with reverence: where he was born, where he awoke, where he first taught, and where he passed away. (paraphrase) Pilgrims still travel to them.
neighbors.difference: Halevi longed for Jerusalem as the land promised to his people, and grieved its ruin. The Buddha's four places mark a teacher's life, and the visit is meant to stir the pilgrim's own practice.
neighbors.shared: a faraway place can hold part of your heart.

neighbors.heading: strangers and pilgrims
neighbors.text: Today Judah Halevi wrote that his heart was in the east while he lived at the end of the west. Christians know a longing like that. The Letter to the Hebrews says of Abraham and his family that they "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth," and that they desired "a better country, that is, an heavenly."
neighbors.difference: Halevi longed for the real land and city, and set sail to reach it. Hebrews turns the longing heavenward: for Christians the country hoped for is with God, though some also travel to Jerusalem as pilgrims.
neighbors.shared: a heart can live in one place and lean toward another.

neighbors.heading: what is up to you
neighbors.text: Today Bahya taught that you can check every box and leave the heart behind, and that the greater war is inside. Stoic philosophers drew a line like that. Epictetus begins his handbook by sorting life in two: what is up to us, like our judgments, desires and aversions, and what isn't, like our bodies, property and reputation. (paraphrase) The real work is the first.
neighbors.difference: Bahya's inner duties face God: trust, love and humility before the One who sees the heart. Epictetus asks for inner discipline as the way to freedom and a calm, good life.
neighbors.shared: the hardest work happens where no one else can see.

neighbors.heading: within, and I abroad
neighbors.text: Today Bahya said a heart can be left behind while the hands do everything right. Saint Augustine confessed that mistake. Looking back on years of searching outside himself, he wrote to God: "Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee." The Church honors him as a Doctor of the Church, a great teacher of the inner life.
neighbors.difference: Bahya teaches inner duties alongside the commandments, and the struggle is with one's own inclination. Augustine tells of being found by God's grace within, and for Catholics that grace comes through Christ.
neighbors.shared: what's inside you matters as much as what your hands do.

neighbors.heading: a woman in the debate
neighbors.text: Today we met Rashi's daughters, learned women whose own words were mostly never written down. Hindu scripture keeps the voice of a woman who asked hard questions out loud. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, at a king's gathering of sages, Gargi Vachaknavi questions the great teacher Yajnavalkya, pressing him on what everything is woven upon. (paraphrase) Her questions stand in the text.
neighbors.difference: Rashi's daughters are known mostly through tradition and the sons they raised. Gargi speaks in the scripture itself, in public debate, in her own name.
neighbors.shared: a learned woman's questions can carry a whole tradition forward.

neighbors.heading: ask Aisha
neighbors.text: Today we met Rashi's daughters, through whom his learning reached the next generation. Muslims remember a woman teacher by name. Aisha, wife of the Prophet, taught long after his death, and many of his sayings come down through her. A companion, Abu Musa, said that whenever the companions were unsure about a hadith, they asked Aisha and found she knew. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Little that Rashi's daughters wrote survives, and much of their story is tradition. Aisha's teaching is recorded in the hadith collections under her own name, and Muslims honor her as a Mother of the Believers.
neighbors.shared: learning can run through a daughter's hands to everyone who comes after.
neighbors.sources: Jami' at-Tirmidhi, chapters on virtues, the report of Abu Musa (paraphrase) · Qur'an 33:6 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: in our own tongue
neighbors.text: Today we heard Yiddish, the mother tongue: the language of the kitchen and the jokes, beside the holy tongue of prayer. Christians tell of a day holy words came in mother tongues. At Pentecost, Acts says, a crowd from many lands heard the apostles and asked: "how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"
neighbors.difference: Yiddish grew as everyday speech, while Hebrew stayed the holy tongue for prayer and study. For Christians, Pentecost is the Holy Spirit's gift, and over the centuries many churches have put scripture and prayer into people's own languages.
neighbors.shared: the language your mother sang in can carry holy things too.

neighbors.heading: the people's speech
neighbors.text: Today we heard Yiddish, the mother tongue, built from many languages and written in Hebrew letters. Sikh scripture speaks the people's speech too. Guru Nanak sang in the everyday language of Punjab, and the Guru Granth Sahib gathers hymns in Punjabi and related tongues, with Persian and Sanskrit words woven in. Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping its script, Gurmukhi.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, Yiddish was the everyday tongue and Hebrew the holy one, kept for prayer and study. For Sikhs, everyday speech became the holy word itself: the Gurus' hymns, sung as gurbani.
neighbors.shared: the words of home can carry the deepest things.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, the languages of gurbani (paraphrase) · Sikh tradition of Guru Angad and Gurmukhi (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: "we lepers"
neighbors.text: Today Abravanel refused to be saved apart from his people. Catholics remember a priest who chose to stay too. Father Damien went to Molokai, the island where people with leprosy were sent away, and lived among them. Tradition says that years later he began a sermon with two words: "we lepers." He had caught the disease, and died among them.
neighbors.difference: Abravanel went with the people he was born among, and couldn't stop the decree. Damien, a priest, chose strangers, served them in Christ's name, and is honored by Catholics as a saint.
neighbors.shared: love sometimes means refusing to be saved alone.
neighbors.sources: Catholic tradition of St. Damien of Molokai (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as long as beings remain
neighbors.text: Today Abravanel refused to be saved apart from his people. Buddhists have a vow with that shape. A bodhisattva seeks awakening for the sake of all beings, not only for themselves. Shantideva, an Indian monk, ends his book with a prayer: as long as space remains and beings remain, may I remain too, to clear away the world's suffering. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Abravanel went into exile with one people, in one terrible year. The bodhisattva's vow reaches every living being, across many lifetimes, and aims at freedom from suffering itself.
neighbors.shared: you don't walk to safety and leave the others behind.

neighbors.heading: watching for the moon
neighbors.text: Today the sages went out at sunset to greet Shabbat like a queen. Muslims go out to greet a holy time too. At the end of Sha'ban, people look to the evening sky for the new crescent that begins Ramadan. The Prophet said: start fasting when you see it, and stop when you see it again. (paraphrase) Then neighbors call out, Ramadan Mubarak.
neighbors.difference: Shabbat comes every week at sunset, greeted with song like a bride. Ramadan comes once a year, a month of fasting, its start marked by the moon; some communities now rely on calculations too.
neighbors.shared: holy time is something you go out to meet.

neighbors.heading: a worshipper of the dawn
neighbors.text: Today the sages walked out to meet Shabbat as a bride. Henry David Thoreau walked out to meet each morning. At Walden Pond he wrote: "I got up early and bathed in the pond; that was a religious exercise, and one of the best things which I did." He called himself a worshipper of Aurora, the dawn, as sincere as the Greeks.
neighbors.difference: Shabbat is greeted together, with set psalms and a song, at sunset each week, as a gift from God. Thoreau's ritual was his own, alone at a pond, honoring the day's renewal.
neighbors.shared: a new beginning feels different when you step outside to meet it.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

neighbors.heading: sing, listen, love
neighbors.text: Today the Hasidim spread joy with melodies sung until a room became one voice. Sikhs gather around song too. Kirtan, singing the Guru's hymns with music, is at the heart of the gurdwara. Guru Nanak's Japji gives the way in: sing, listen, and keep love in your mind. (paraphrase) The sangat, the gathered community, sings together, and the sound fills the hall.
neighbors.difference: A Hasidic niggun is often sung without words, with joy as a way to serve God. In Sikh kirtan the words lead: the hymns are gurbani, the Guru's own word, set to ragas.
neighbors.shared: singing together can turn a crowd into a family.
neighbors.sources: Japji Sahib, pauri 5, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: singing the name
neighbors.text: Today the Hasidim spread joy with melodies and crowded tables. Hindus know that joy as bhakti, loving devotion, and it often sings. In Bengal, Chaitanya led crowds through the streets singing the names of Krishna. The Bhagavata Purana pictures a devotee so moved by God's names that they laugh, weep, sing aloud and dance, past caring what the world thinks. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Hasidic joy grew inside Jewish law and study, gathered around a rebbe's table. Bhakti singing often centers on a beloved form of God, like Krishna, and the name itself is felt to carry God's presence.
neighbors.shared: joy, shared out loud, can carry people closer to God.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana 11.2.40 (paraphrase) · the sankirtan tradition of Chaitanya (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: straightening the arrow
neighbors.text: Today Rabbi Salanter asked people to work on their own character, one trait at a time. Buddhists train the mind with the same patience. The Dhammapada says: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back."
neighbors.difference: Mussar works on character as service to God, through the Torah's ethical teachings, line by line. Buddhist mind training aims to end suffering, through meditation and watching the mind, without leaning on a creator God.
neighbors.shared: you can change slowly, one honest step at a time.

neighbors.heading: add to your faith
neighbors.text: Today Rabbi Salanter taught people to work on one trait at a time, the way a craftsman fixes one seam, then the next. A Christian letter builds a ladder like that: "add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience," and on, step by step, up to charity, which is love.
neighbors.difference: Mussar asks for steady self-work, reading and repeating ethical lines until they reach the heart. Christians speak of the same growth as God's grace at work in them, which they answer with their own effort.
neighbors.shared: becoming good is slow work, and it's never too late to start.

neighbors.heading: room for a kindness
neighbors.text: Today, as Passover ended, Muslim neighbors in Morocco brought flour and butter, and Jewish homes opened their doors. The Roman philosopher Seneca saw every neighbor as a chance like that. He wrote that wherever there is a human being, there is room for a kindness. (paraphrase) For the Stoics, people of every city also belong to one great human city.
neighbors.difference: Mimouna has its own night, foods and blessings, and acts out the Torah's command to love your neighbor. Seneca's kindness is a habit of reason and character, with no set day, owed to anyone at all.
neighbors.shared: an open door is a blessing for both sides of it.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, On the Happy Life 24 (paraphrase) · Seneca, On Leisure 4 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you took me in
neighbors.text: Today, as Passover ended, Moroccan Jewish homes opened their doors, and neighbors came in to eat. Catholics are taught to look for Jesus in the guest. In Matthew he says to those who welcomed others: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Saint Benedict's Rule for monks says to receive every guest as Christ himself. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Mimouna's open door acts out the Torah's love of neighbor, and welcomes neighbors of another faith. For Catholics, welcome means meeting Christ in the guest, whoever they are.
neighbors.shared: the person at your door is worth getting up for.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 53 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: turning toward one place
neighbors.text: Today Beta Israel climbed a hill and prayed toward Jerusalem, a city they had never seen. Muslims turn toward one place in every prayer, from anywhere on earth: the Kaaba in Mecca. The Qur'an says: "wheresoever ye may be, turn your faces (when ye pray) toward it." And the hadith say the earliest Muslims first prayed toward Jerusalem.
neighbors.difference: Jews face Jerusalem, the city of the Temple, and pray to return there. Muslims face the Kaaba, which they trace to Abraham, and hope to see it once, on the hajj.
neighbors.shared: people far apart can lean toward the same holy point.

neighbors.heading: the holy crossing
neighbors.text: Today Beta Israel fasted, climbed a high place, and prayed toward a city far away. Hindus know the pull of holy places too. Pilgrims travel to a tirtha, a crossing place, often a river ford or a mountain, where heaven feels near. The Mahabharata gives whole chapters to the holy fords, and praises the journey as open even to those who can't afford great rites. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Sigd faces one city, Jerusalem, and renews a covenant with the one God of the Torah. Hindu pilgrimage has many holy places, rivers, mountains and temple towns, and the journey itself is part of the worship.
neighbors.shared: a holy place far away can shape how you stand today.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, the tirtha-yatra chapters (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the cries of the workers
neighbors.text: Today we honored young workers trapped behind a locked factory door, and the laws that followed. The Letter of James speaks for workers like them: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."
neighbors.difference: The Torah gives direct laws: pay wages the same day, and don't stand by your neighbor's blood. James warns the rich in a prophet's voice, and Christians read it alongside Jesus's care for the poor.
neighbors.shared: the people who do the work are seen, even when they're unseen.

neighbors.heading: the bread of honest work
neighbors.text: Today we honored workers who died behind a locked door, and the fight for their safety that followed. Sikhs tell a story about workers' bread. Guru Nanak chose to eat at the home of Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter, over the feast of Malik Bhago, a rich official. Sikhs tell that when he squeezed the two breads, Lalo's gave milk and Bhago's gave blood.
neighbors.difference: The Torah gives laws: pay workers on time, and don't stand by when a neighbor is in danger. The Sikh story teaches through a remembered story, and Sikhs live it as kirat karni, earning by honest work.
neighbors.shared: honest work deserves honor, and a safe way home.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: mother of immigrants
neighbors.text: Today Henrietta Szold taught immigrants at night, after their long days of work, and then built care for mothers and children. Catholics remember a woman with a life like hers. Frances Xavier Cabrini, an Italian nun, came to New York to serve Italian immigrants, and founded schools, orphanages and hospitals. The Church named her a saint, and patron of immigrants.
neighbors.difference: Szold's work echoed the Torah's "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children," and built a Jewish women's organization. Cabrini founded an order of sisters, and Catholics ask her prayers for immigrants.
neighbors.shared: a newcomer learning a new language deserves a patient teacher.
neighbors.sources: Catholic tradition of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini (paraphrase) · Deuteronomy 6:7 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: for the welfare of the many
neighbors.text: Today Henrietta Szold taught in every room she entered: night classes, books, rescued children. Buddhists remember a teacher who sent teachers out. The Buddha told his first monks: "Go ye now, O Bhikkhus, and wander, for the gain of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world."
neighbors.difference: Szold's teaching echoed the Torah's command to teach your children, stretched wide to strangers. The Buddha sent monks to teach a path out of suffering, open to anyone who would listen.
neighbors.shared: teaching is one of the kindest gifts one person gives another.
neighbors.sources: Vinaya, Mahavagga I.11 (Rhys Davids and Oldenberg)

neighbors.heading: sharing with newcomers
neighbors.text: Today we met the kibbutz, where members held everything in common and shared the work. Muslims remember a time of sharing like it. When the Prophet's companions fled to Medina, the people there took them in as brothers, sharing homes and harvests. The Qur'an praises those who "prefer (the fugitives) above themselves though poverty become their lot."
neighbors.difference: The kibbutz made shared property a whole way of life, a farm with a common purse. Medina's sharing was brotherhood among believers in a hard time; Islam keeps private property, with zakat and charity as duties.
neighbors.shared: a hard life gets lighter when people carry it together.

neighbors.heading: made for cooperation
neighbors.text: Today we met the kibbutz, where people shared the work, the meals and the meeting. The emperor and philosopher Marcus Aurelius wrote a thought like it, in a note to himself about starting the day: "For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth." Working against each other, he says, goes against nature.
neighbors.difference: The kibbutz built cooperation into daily life: shared money, meals and decisions, with a dream of a people gathered home. Marcus treats cooperation as a law of nature and reason, to be lived wherever you are.
neighbors.shared: we were made to need each other, and that's good news.

neighbors.heading: the light in every one
neighbors.text: Today six million became six million worlds, each one complete. Sikhs sing at night of a light inside every person. In Kirtan Sohila, Guru Nanak says: the light within everyone is Your light, and by its shining, everyone shines. (paraphrase) In that hymn, no one is only a number. Each person carries the same light.
neighbors.difference: The Mishnah teaches each life's worth from one person created alone: each soul is a whole world. Guru Nanak's hymn finds that worth in the one divine light shining in everyone.
neighbors.shared: each life is whole, and no one is only a number.
neighbors.sources: Kirtan Sohila, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 13 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the same self in all
neighbors.text: Today six million became six million worlds, each one complete. Hindu scripture teaches a way of seeing that makes no one a stranger. The Isha Upanishad says that one who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, turns away from no one. (paraphrase) The Bhagavad Gita says the wise look with an equal eye on every creature. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: The Mishnah begins with one human being created alone, so each person is a world. The Upanishad begins with one Self present in all beings, so harming another is never harming a stranger.
neighbors.shared: every face in a crowd is a whole world.

neighbors.heading: as a mother protects
neighbors.text: Today we met the Righteous, people who hid and saved Jews at the risk of their own lives. Buddhists keep a teaching about that kind of love. The Metta Sutta says to hold all beings in a boundless heart, the way a mother protects her only child with her own life. (paraphrase) Not some beings. All of them.
neighbors.difference: The Tosefta honors the righteous of every nation for what they did. The Metta Sutta trains a heart of love meant to reach every being without limit, long before any knock at the door.
neighbors.shared: when someone knocks, an open door can save a world.

neighbors.heading: who is my neighbor
neighbors.text: Today we met the Righteous, among them a pastor, André Trocmé, whose village took in Jewish children. Jesus told a story about crossing a line to help. In Luke, a man lies beaten by the road, and a Samaritan, a stranger, "had compassion on him, And went to him, and bound up his wounds." Then Jesus says: "Go, and do thou likewise."
neighbors.difference: The Righteous risked their lives, and came from many faiths and none. In Luke, Jesus tells the Samaritan story to answer a question about the Torah's command to love your neighbor.
neighbors.shared: a neighbor is anyone you choose to help.

neighbors.heading: yes to life anyway
neighbors.text: Today the tradition turned from mourning back toward life: choose life, l'chaim. Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived the camps, taught something close. He taught that even in great suffering a person can find meaning, and keeps the freedom to choose how to meet it. (paraphrase) A book of his is titled, in German, say yes to life in spite of everything.
neighbors.difference: Choose life is a command from God, lived through law and blessing: a wedding goes first, a toast, a table. Frankl offers it as a finding about people: meaning can be found by anyone, of any faith or none.
neighbors.shared: after great loss, choosing life is a kind of courage.
neighbors.sources: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning; ...trotzdem Ja zum Leben sagen (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: life more abundantly
neighbors.text: Today the tradition turned back toward life: the wedding goes first, and the toast is l'chaim, to life. Catholics hear a promise of life too. In John's Gospel, Jesus says: "I am come that they may have life, and may have it more abundantly." The Church teaches that every human life is sacred.
neighbors.difference: Deuteronomy's choose life is a call to keep the covenant and live, here and now. Catholics hear Jesus's words as life with God, which they believe death can't end.
neighbors.shared: life is a gift worth choosing again each day.
neighbors.sources: John 10:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2258 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: every act an offering
neighbors.text: Today Abraham Joshua Heschel marched at Selma and said his legs were praying. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna tells Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. (paraphrase) Gandhi, who drew deeply on the Gita, led marches of his own.
neighbors.difference: Heschel's march grew from the Hebrew prophets, who cry out when the poor are crushed. The Gita teaches action offered to God without clinging to its fruits, as a path of yoga.
neighbors.shared: a walk for someone else's dignity can be a prayer.

neighbors.heading: change it with your hand
neighbors.text: Today Heschel marched at Selma and said his legs were praying. Muslims are taught to answer wrong with action too. The Prophet said: whoever sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he can't, with his tongue; if he can't, then in his heart. (paraphrase) And the Qur'an says: "Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah."
neighbors.difference: Heschel's march grew from the prophets' cry for the poor, walking beside a Christian pastor's movement. The hadith ranks the responses, hand, tongue, heart, and calls the last the weakest faith.
neighbors.shared: standing up for others can be part of worship.

neighbors.heading: and many others
neighbors.text: Today we heard that women were always there, even when nobody was taking notes. Luke's Gospel stops to name some of them. Traveling with Jesus were Mary Magdalene, "And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance." Later, women came first to the empty tomb.
neighbors.difference: Much of women's lives in Jewish history went unwritten, and historians gather the traces. The Gospels name women among Jesus's followers, and Christians honor them as the first witnesses of the resurrection.
neighbors.shared: the people keeping it all going deserve to be named.

neighbors.heading: Mata Khivi's kitchen
neighbors.text: Today we heard that women were always there, keeping the whole thing alive. Sikhs remember one by name in their scripture. Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad, served in the langar, the free kitchen where everyone sits and eats together. A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib praises her goodness, like a leafy tree giving deep shade, and the rich kheer she served. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Women's work in Jewish history often went unwritten, and is being gathered now. Sikh scripture itself names Mata Khivi, and the langar she served still runs in gurdwaras, open to anyone.
neighbors.shared: a meal made with love can hold a whole community together.
neighbors.sources: Ramkali ki Var of Satta and Balvand, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 967 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no more strangers
neighbors.text: Today we learned that someone who chose Judaism is fully Jewish, and must never be reminded of their past. Catholics welcome newcomers with a line from Ephesians: "you are no more strangers and foreigners; but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and the domestics of God." Adults who join the Church are received completely, not halfway.
neighbors.difference: In Judaism a convert joins a people as well as a faith, like Ruth, ancestor of David. For Catholics a newcomer joins through baptism, entering what they call the body of Christ.
neighbors.shared: whoever has come home belongs, with no footnote.

neighbors.heading: rivers into the sea
neighbors.text: Today we learned that a person who chose Judaism is fully Jewish, and their past is never thrown at them. The Buddha gave a picture of the same welcome. Great rivers, he said, lose their old names when they reach the ocean and are simply called the ocean. So too, people of every caste who join the order leave their old names behind. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: Jewish tradition welcomes a convert into a people and a covenant, with Ruth as the model. The Buddha's picture is about the monastic order, where old caste names are set aside on the path to awakening.
neighbors.shared: where you came from never makes you less at home.

neighbors.heading: deeds that keep going
neighbors.text: Today a yahrzeit candle burned, and families gave charity and studied in a loved one's name. Muslims believe a life's good can keep going too. The Prophet said that when a person dies, their deeds end except three: charity that keeps on giving, knowledge that benefits others, and a righteous child who prays for them. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: The yahrzeit keeps a set date each year, with a candle and a Kaddish that praises God. The hadith sets no yearly day for this; in Islam, prayer and charity for the dead can come any day.
neighbors.shared: love keeps doing good in the name of someone gone.

neighbors.heading: what i learned from them
neighbors.text: Today a candle burned for someone gone, and someone told a story about them. Marcus Aurelius began his private notebook the same way: with the people who shaped him, one by one. "From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper." Then his mother, his teachers, his friends, each with the gift they left him.
neighbors.difference: The yahrzeit returns on a set date, with a candle and the Kaddish, praising God among the community. Marcus kept his remembering as private writing, a thank-you list, with no fixed day.
neighbors.shared: the people we've lost are still teaching us.

neighbors.heading: the same light
neighbors.text: Today the Kedushah came down to earth: from generation to generation, holiness handed on. Sikhs speak of a handing-on too. The light of Guru Nanak passed from one Guru to the next. A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib says it: the same light, the same way, only the body changed. (paraphrase) In time, the Guru's light passed to the scripture itself.
neighbors.difference: L'dor vador hands holiness from parents to children, each generation answering back. For Sikhs the passing ran Guru to Guru, and since Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru.
neighbors.shared: what we're given is ours to hand on.
neighbors.sources: Ramkali ki Var of Satta and Balvand, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 966 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: handed down in succession
neighbors.text: Today we heard l'dor vador: from generation to generation, holiness handed on. Hindus call that kind of handing-on parampara, a line of teachers. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that this yoga was handed down in succession, known by royal sages, then lost over long time, so he teaches it again. (paraphrase)
neighbors.difference: In the Kedushah, the passing is between generations of a people: parents, children, a congregation answering. Parampara usually runs teacher to student, and in the Gita, God himself restores what was lost.
neighbors.shared: every generation is a link, and every link matters.
